content: It is challenging to establish and develop prosthetics and orthotics services. According to Article 32 of the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD), international cooperation, particularly in the form of technology and knowledge transfer, is crucial. This collaboration can accelerate the development of these services, especially in lowand middle-income countries. Governments and other stakeholders must ensure they stay informed about international advancements in prosthetics and orthotics to apply evidence-based best practices in their national service delivery systems. Sharing local experiences with the global prosthetics and orthotics community enhances collective knowledge at an international level. Organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO) and the International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics (ISPO), along with higher education institutions, can facilitate the exchange of research findings and evidence-based practices. Governments and national stakeholders should engage in international collaboration to share experiences, data, and research related to prosthetics and orthotics service provision. Support from international organizations and non-governmental organizations (NGOs) plays a vital role in establishing and strengthening prosthetics and orthotics services and professional training. Such support is most effective when aligned with national health and welfare policies and strategic plans or when it contributes to their development if they do not already exist. International organizations are more likely to achieve sustainable, long-term results when they work within and strengthen national systems, contributing to their further development. This requires expertise not only in technical aspects of service provision but also in policy-making, systems development, sector planning, and financing. When international support is provided, it should contribute to the establishment and implementation of national prosthetics and orthotics policies and strategic plans. It must also align with the national health and welfare service provision system. Universal health coverage aims to ensure that all individuals can access necessary health services, including prosthetics and orthotics, without financial hardship. Sustainable funding must be available to provide these services to all in need. Planning and budgeting should be based on a comprehensive analysis of costs and benefits. The economic implications of prosthetics and orthotics service provision are often poorly understood by policymakers. However, detailed cost information is essential for assessing the financial requirements of providing prosthetics and orthotics to a population. At the national level, costs should be analyzed across five key areas: service establishment, human resource training, service provision, user expenses, and system monitoring. These areas encompass the full cost of prosthetics and orthotics treatment, highlighting the financial resources needed to support the population. At the service level, data on the full cost of each type of treatment and product enables accurate pricing and budgeting. Investment in prosthetics and orthotics services yields financial returns for individuals, their families, caregivers, and society as a whole, as healthier individuals require less support and many can return to work. Both individuals and society benefit, and the financial return on investment in this sector is a compelling argument for service provision. The financial implications are best understood by comparing the economic benefits with the required investment. Comprehensive data on costs and benefits allow relevant ministries, such as those for health, social welfare, and finance, to make informed decisions for planning and budgeting prosthetics and orthotics services. They can also recognize that the cost burden on one ministry may be offset by savings in another. The cost of providing prosthetics and orthotics services should be periodically assessed. Both the direct and indirect economic benefits of these services should be analyzed at individual, family, community, societal, health sector, and national levels. Governments and stakeholders must have access to reliable data on the total and unmet needs for prosthetics and orthotics to plan and monitor the sector effectively. Accurate data on national needs for these services are rarely available, but information on how many people require services, the types of services needed, and their geographic distribution is essential for planning and developing nationwide services. Most users require their prosthesis or orthosis for life, with regular replacements, which must be considered when collecting data. Data are also necessary for monitoring service provision to understand how many people have access to services and who they are. This information allows verification of the quality, effectiveness, and efficiency of services and ensures that improvements can be made. For service units, data are best collected during routine operations using existing user management systems. Much of this information is valuable for monitoring prosthetics and orthotics service provision to evaluate whether they are developing according to national plans. Establishing a national database on service provision and outcomes will facilitate data collection, monitoring, analysis, and the exchange and comparison of data among service providers. The general population, including health workers and potential service users, is often unaware of the purpose and benefits of prosthetics and orthotics services. As a result, many individuals who need these services are excluded and experience poor health. Raising awareness and promoting these services is as important as any other health program. Governments are obligated to provide accessible information about these services to people with disabilities, including information about mobility aids, devices, and assistive technologies such as prostheses and orthoses. All stakeholders, including users and service providers, should work to raise awareness about policies and referral systems. When the need, role, and benefits of prosthetics and orthotics services are explained, they become more visible and accessible to new user groups. Awareness-raising campaigns are more effective when they target diverse audiences and use rights-based, social, and economic arguments. A range of prosthetic and orthotic products, with varying components, materials, and working methods, is required to meet the diverse needs of users. Services may provide combinations of basic, intermediate, and advanced products that are either prefabricated or custom-made, locally available, or imported. The complexity of services ranges from providing an off-the-shelf product fitted in one session to custom-made products that may take days or weeks to fabricate. Products and methods should be appropriate to the setting in which they are fabricated, fitted, used, and funded to ensure accessibility for all. Products are considered appropriate when they provide proper fit and alignment, meet the individual’s needs, and can be sustained by the country at the most economical price. Nationally agreed criteria help assess the appropriateness of available options and ensure that service providers offer the best mix and range of products for the local context. A national list of priority prosthetic and orthotic products, as part of a broader list of priority assistive products, helps governments fulfill their commitment to ensuring access to high-quality assistive products at an affordable cost, as mandated by the CRPD. Such a list, combined with appropriate financing, improves access to assistive products, including prostheses and orthoses. A national classification of prosthetics and orthotics based on the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) classification harmonizes prescription practices and facilitates the exchange of information on prosthetics and orthotics nationally and internationally. A range of components, materials, and consumables is required to fabricate prostheses and orthoses. Some can be sourced locally, while others must be imported. To fabricate high-quality prostheses and orthoses efficiently, service units require high-quality components, materials, consumables, tools, machines, and other equipment, some of which are often imported. In many countries, the cost of the final prosthesis or orthosis is significantly increased by high import duties and taxes on imported supplies. Exemption from import duties and customs fees for items used exclusively to fabricate prostheses and orthoses, which are not available locally, contributes to lowering prices and enables the fabrication of high-quality products at an affordable cost. The reuse of prosthetic and orthotic components must be properly monitored to prevent the use of low-quality, overused, or defective items, which could result in accidents and injuries. Regulation by a designated authority or group of experts, along with refurbishment of items under controlled conditions, ensures user safety. Components, materials, consumables, tools, machines, and other equipment used exclusively for fabricating prosthetic and orthotic products that are not available locally should be exempt from import duties and customs fees. The reuse of prosthetic and orthotic components should be regulated by a designated authority or group of experts with no conflicts of interest, involving proper quality control and documentation.
